means:
To come to an end, or to bring something to an end.

*Stop* is the everyday word and works on anything, including a single motion — *stop the car*. **Cease** is its formal cousin, and it wants something **ongoing**: fire, trading, operations, breathing, rain, publication. It carries the tone of an announcement or an order — treaties, legal notices, official statements. "Cease immediately" is what an authority writes; "cut it out" is what a person says. It also leans final: things that cease tend not to resume.

Note the fixed phrase **never ceases to** — *he never ceases to amaze me* — one of the few places the word sounds casual.
trap: ⚠️ **cease ≠ seize.** *Cease* (SEES) is to **stop**; *seize* (SEEZ) is to **grab**. Near-opposites, one letter apart — and the spelling breaks the "i before e" rule in *seize*, which is why people mix them up on the page.
trick_line: **The de-CEASED has ceased.** And **in-cessant** noise never does.
trick_unpack: Both cousins point the same way: *deceased* is the formal word for stopped-for-good, and *incessant* is literally "not ceasing" — the register stays official in every one of them.
sentences: Trading on the exchange **ceased** at noon and did not resume for three days.
He **never ceases to** amaze me — third time this month he's locked himself out.
in_the_wild: A **cease and desist** letter — the lawyer's opening move, telling you to stop doing the thing *and* never start again. And every news **ceasefire**: the fire ceases, the war doesn't necessarily end.
etymology: Latin **cedere** = *"to go, to yield, to give way"* → **cessare**, "to leave off." Yielding ground is the common thread across a big GRE family: **cede** (hand over), **concede**, **recede**, **precede**, **secede**, **cessation**, **incessant**, **deceased**.
one_line: To stop or come to an end — formal register.
root: cedere, cessare (to yield, to leave off)
